Email Manager

Your inbox, answered from the chat you’re already in.

Try saying

Reply to Dana and say I’ll have it over by FridayAnything from Jack this week?

Every add-on is included with Archie.

Download Archie
More about Email Manager

Ask and it looks. "What's my latest email?", "anything from Jack this week?", "what did I send Todd about the invoice?" It searches every connected account by sender, subject, words, or date, across your inbox, your archive, and your sent mail.

Ask it to reply and it drafts. "Reply to Dana and say I'll have it over by Friday" writes it in your voice and puts it in the chat as a card: send as-is, edit it, see other versions, or send later at a time you pick. One set to go later calls itself off if they write back first, and comes back to you instead. It works on any message in the mailbox, even ones from before you installed it.

Or start one from nothing. "Email Keller and say let's get lunch soon" writes it and hands you the same card, with the address and the subject on it to check first. Give it an address and it uses that one. Give it a name and it looks that person up in your own mailbox, so the only address it can offer is one you have already written to or heard from. Finding nobody, it asks you for the address rather than guessing.

Meanwhile it watches. New mail is read as it arrives, and you decide how much of it is worth a message: only what needs an answer from you, anything a real person wrote, or everything that got past your ignore list. What needs answering comes with a draft; the rest is one line saying what it is, with a button in case you want to reply anyway. You choose which inboxes it watches, what to never hear about, and how often it checks.

If you checked Let it tidy up, it can move mail out of your inbox, which is your mail app's archive and puts back in one word. It can never delete anything.

Works with any email account connected on the agent's Connections tab, under Email, calendar, files.

Calendar Manager

Your calendar, without opening your calendar.

Every add-on is included with Archie.

Download Archie
More about Calendar Manager

Your agent reads your calendar, on Google or Outlook, and drafts changes to it in chat. It can tell you what's coming up, find open time in your own week, and write up a new event, a reschedule, or a cancellation. Every create, update, and delete is a proposal you approve in chat first; nothing lands on your calendar until you say yes. Two limits worth knowing before you install. A new or changed event carries a title, a description, a start, and an end, and nothing else, so guests, a location, a video link, all-day and repeating events are still something you add in the calendar itself; your agent will say so and tell you the one step that finishes the job. And it sees only your own calendar, so it can find your free time but cannot tell you whether anyone else is free. Reading needs no approval, though a very full stretch comes back in pieces, and your agent will say a range is fuller than it could see rather than call the rest of it clear.

I'll take the Meyer quoteWhat's open?

See Archie for Business
More about Who's Got This

Small teams lose work in the gap between “someone should” and “I did”, and the owner ends up as the router who remembers who took what. This hands that over. When somebody claims a piece of work in the team's chat, the agent files it: what it is, who has it, when it was raised, and the due date if one was said. When work is raised and nobody takes it, that gets a row too, with the owner blank, and blank owners lead every report because unclaimed is where work goes to die. Ask “what's open?”, “what's on Dana?”, or “who's got the Meyer quote?” and get one line per row, longest-open first, with ages counted honestly. Handing a thing to someone else moves the row and keeps the history. Done is said, not assumed: a row closes when its owner says so, and until then its age is the fact you see. The agent never nags anyone; it keeps the ledger true and reports it when asked.

Airtable Keeper

Your Airtable, filed and searched without opening it.

Try saying

What bases can you see?

Every add-on is included with Archie.

Download Archie
More about Airtable Keeper

An Airtable base starts as a good idea and turns into a museum. Rows go in and nobody closes them, a status column stops matching what actually happened, and the view you built in March answers a question you no longer ask.

The work is not typing rows. It is keeping what you already typed true, and that is the part nobody does.

Connect Airtable and your agent works the real base. Ask what is in a table and it reads the live rows. Tell it to file something and it finds the table, reads the columns that actually exist, and builds the row from those instead of guessing at names. Ask what has gone stale and it sorts by when each row last changed and tells you what nobody has touched.

It remembers where things live, so the second question about a table costs no searching. Changes are shown to you before they happen.

Works with

  • Airtable

Setting up Airtable Keeper

  1. Make the token at Airtable, at airtable.com/create/tokens. Check schema.bases:read and data.records:read, plus data.records:write if you want your agent to be able to add or change a row.
  2. On the same screen, under Access, add each base you want your agent to work with. A token with every scope and no bases added can see nothing at all, and every call comes back refused. This is the step people miss.

Made by Otian AI.

More about Form Filler

Forty fields, and you have answered every one of them before. Address, dates, policy numbers, the same three paragraphs about what you do. Forms are a pure tax, and the reason nobody automates them is that every form is different.

This fills them the way a person would: it reads the actual page, works out what each field is asking for, and answers from what your agent already knows about you. Where it does not know something, it asks you once and remembers, so the next form that asks is free.

It always stops at Submit. You see the finished screen before anything becomes real, and pressing the button is yours. It never touches password or payment fields, and if a form wants a sign-in code it hands the window straight back to you.

That is also where it compounds: a form is a questionnaire about your life, so every one it fills teaches it facts it did not have, and it gets faster at the next one on its own.

What Form Filler needs

Needs Computer control turned on, which is off until you switch it on. Your agent works the site in a browser window on your own computer, and you can watch it. It never types a password or a card you pay with, and it asks before pressing anything that finalizes.

Works with

  • Gitlab

Setting up GitLab Keeper

  1. Make the token at GitLab, under your avatar, Preferences, Access tokens. Check read_api if you only want your agent to read, or api if you want it to be able to post a comment.
  2. The read-only scope cannot comment, and when it tries, the failure reads like a permission problem on the project rather than on the token. Make a new token with api checked and connect that one.

Made by Otian AI.

It opens by counting, not by asking. The first thing it does is go through your inbox and come back with the piles: how many from each sender, how many you never opened. Nobody knows they have 214 emails from one bank, which is why the tidying never gets done.

More about Job Hunt

A hunt is thirty applications across eight hiring systems, each with its own login, and a mailbox where the confirmation, the interview invite and the rejection for the same job are four weeks apart. Nobody can see the shape of that from inside it. This keeps one list: what you applied for, where each one got to, and what the posting actually said, saved before the listing comes down and takes the requirements and the salary band with it.

It fills the list from your mail rather than asking you to. Every hiring system sends a confirmation when you apply, a scheduling mail when they want to talk, and a rejection when they do not, and it reads all three and moves the row itself. Ask how it is going and you get the count at each stage and, if the numbers are big enough to mean anything, which stage is the one leaking: many applications and no screens is a different problem from screens that never become offers, and only one of them is fixed by applying to more places.

It drafts follow-ups and never sends them, and it will not apply for anything or answer an offer on your behalf.

Reading your mail needs an email account connected on the agent's Connections tab, under Email, calendar, files. Without one it still keeps the list from what you tell it.

More about Linear Keeper

Linear is where the work is written down, and the cost of that is a tab you have to go and open. What is assigned to me, what moved while I was in meetings, what is due Friday, what did somebody say on that issue: every one of those is a trip to a board and a bit of scanning, and the answer is usually four lines long.

Connect Linear and your agent reads the board instead. Ask what is waiting on you and it comes back with the issues assigned to you that are not finished, in the order they last moved, with the status in your team's own words and the ones that are late at the top. Ask what changed this week and it says what changed and who changed it. Ask about one issue and it reads the description and the comments and tells you where it stands.

It can open an issue, move one, reassign one, and leave a comment too, and every one of those is shown to you before it happens. Nothing lands on your team's board without you saying yes.

Works with

  • Linear

Setting up Linear Keeper

  1. Make the key in Linear, under Settings, Account, Security and access, then Personal API keys. Give it Read plus Write if you want your agent to be able to propose a change; Read alone answers every question here.
  2. A key can be limited to certain teams. One that is will answer about those teams and nothing else, and an issue outside them comes back as a permission error rather than as missing.
  3. Paste it in Archie on the Connections tab, then Apps, beside Linear.

More about Notion Keeper

Notion is where good intentions go to sit. Pages get made and never finished, statuses stay on "In progress" for four months, and the database you set up in January is now a museum. The work is not writing things down; it is keeping what you wrote down true.

Connect Notion and your agent works the workspace you already have, not a copy of it. Say "put this in my reading list" and it finds the right database, reads what columns it actually has, and fills them in. Ask "what's in my project tracker?" and it reads back what is really there. Say "mark the Henderson project done" and it shows you the exact change before it touches anything. Ask "what's gone quiet in Notion?" and it tells you which rows nobody has touched in weeks, which is the question no Notion view answers well.

The first time you use it, it looks around and shows you what it can see, so you are never guessing whether it is connected. Nothing is mirrored into Archie, so there is no second copy to drift out of date.

More about Exec Concierge

Exec Concierge is Concise with a point of view. It leads with the answer, keeps every reply scannable, and then does the thing a plain summary will not: when there is a choice on the table it says which option it would take and gives the one line of reasoning behind it, because you asked precisely so you would not have to weigh it yourself. It filters as hard as it reports. Whatever it can handle without you gets handled and mentioned in a clause, and only the items that genuinely need a decision get a line of their own. Ask for a draft and the draft is in the reply, not a promise of one. Anything that cannot be taken back stops first: sending, deleting, declining and spending each get one short line and a wait.
